Short case 21 · General Surgery

Testicular Tumour

A solid, heavy testis in a young man that you cannot feel separately from the swelling, with lost testicular sensation and a normal vas. That is the case. The marks are in what you do next: ultrasound and markers before you operate, an inguinal incision and never a scrotal one, and para-aortic nodes rather than inguinal ones.

S Das: clinical method Bailey & Love: mechanism and management SRB: exam framework

1The three numbers to open with

How common, and how malignant
All three books agree on the headline. S Das: "though these tumours only constitute 1% of all malignant tumours in man, yet these are one of the commonest forms of malignant tumours in the young. Almost all (99%) testicular tumours are malignant."Das 40 · p.630 SRB repeats both figures.SRB 26 · p.1070 B&L: "testicular cancer represents around 1 to 1.5% of male neoplasms", with "3 to 10 new cases per 100 000 males per year in western societies", and "they are the commonest form of tumour in young men."B&L 86 · p.1569
Why "99% malignant" is the one to sayBecause it is the justification for everything that follows. There is no safe period of observation and no place for a needle. A solid intratesticular mass is treated as cancer until the histology says otherwise.
Germ cell or not
Germ cell tumours are 90 to 95%.B&L 86 · p.1569 SRB puts germ cell at 95% and non-germ-cell at 5%.SRB 26 · p.1070 Everything else, lymphoma, sex cord-stromal tumours, secondaries, shares the remainder.
Bilateral, and the figure differs slightly
B&L: "in 1 to 2% of cases the tumour is bilateral at diagnosis."B&L 86 · p.1571 SRB: "3% of testicular tumours are bilateral."SRB 26 · p.1072 Say 1 to 3% and you are safe in either room. The practical consequence is the same in both books: ultrasound the other testis too.
And one genetic marker worth naming
"A specific genetic marker, an isochromosome of the short arm of chromosome 12 (i12p), is pathognomonic of all types of adult GCTs as well as germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS)."B&L 86 · p.1569 GCNIS is the term that has replaced carcinoma in situ of the testis; if you say it, say it as germ cell neoplasia in situ.

2History: what to ask and what each answer buys

1. How old? Because the two main tumours sit in different decades. S Das: "teratoma occurs between the ages of 20 and 30 years, whereas seminoma occurs between the ages of 30 and 50 years."Das 40 · p.630 B&L: "the peak incidence of seminomas is in the fourth decade of life, with the non-seminomatous germ cell tumours (NSGCT) being more common in the third decade of life."B&L 86 · p.1569 The rule that survives bothYounger means teratoma or NSGCT, older means seminoma. Both books put the crossover around 30. Lymphoma of the testis is the tumour of the man over 50, and spermatocytic seminoma is seen "only in adult men usually over 50 years old".B&L 86 · p.1570
2. How did it come to notice, and how long? "The commonest presentation is a painless swelling of the testis. Duration is about a few months. Trivial injury may draw the attention of the patient towards the swelling and he often incriminates trauma to be the cause."Das 40 · p.630 B&L: "occasionally, an episode of trauma calls attention to the swelling."B&L 86 · p.1571 The trap, and it is a common oneA man presents after a minor knock to the scrotum with a swelling he blames on the injury. The trauma did not cause the tumour; it made him examine himself. Accepting the patient's attribution is how these diagnoses get delayed, and saying this sentence aloud in a viva is worth a mark.
3. Is there pain? Usually not, and that is itself the point. B&L: "a sensation of heaviness can occur if large, but few patients experience pain."B&L 86 · p.1571 SRB puts pain in the testis at 30%.SRB 26 · p.1071 S Das: "dull aching or dragging pain may be experienced in the scrotum if the swelling has grown very large."Das 40 · p.630 The presentation that gets misdiagnosedBoth books warn of it. B&L: "some cases may simulate epididymo-orchitis and, rarely, acute painful enlargement of the testis occurs because of haemorrhage into the tumour, which can mimic testicular torsion."B&L 86 · p.1571 S Das: "acute pain and tenderness is very rare form of presentation which is indistinguishable from acute epididymo-orchitis."Das 40 · p.630 So an epididymo-orchitis that does not settle on antibiotics must be imaged, not re-treated.
4. Has he ever had an undescended testis, or an operation for one? It is the one risk factor that changes the whole conversation. B&L's epidemiological risk factors are "cryptorchidism, male factor infertility (including Klinefelter syndrome), familial history of testicular tumours among first-grade relatives and the presence of a contralateral tumour or GCNIS".B&L 86 · p.1569 SRB's predisposing factors are undescended testis and testicular atrophy.SRB 26 · p.1070 And look at the other side of the scrotumSRB gives the sign: "hemiscrotum with absence of rugae with suspicious mass in the groin suggests undescended testis with testicular tumour."SRB 26 · p.1072 An empty, smooth hemiscrotum plus an inguinal or abdominal mass is a tumour in an undescended testis, and SRB illustrates exactly that case being removed through a suprainguinal approach.SRB 26 · p.1072 How much does it raise the risk?The books differ sharply, by an order of magnitude. See the amber box.
5. Any symptom of spread? Because occasionally that is the presentation. B&L: "rarely, the predominant symptoms are those of metastatic disease. Intra-abdominal disease may cause abdominal or lumbar pain. Lung metastases are usually silent, but they can cause chest pain, dyspnoea and haemoptysis in the later stages... the primary tumour may not have been noticed by the patient, and indeed may be detected only by ultrasound."B&L 86 · p.1571 S Das: "rarely this condition may present itself as abdominal pain and swelling of the legs due to secondary metastasis in the pre- and para-aortic groups of lymph nodes."Das 40 · p.630 Why the legs swellBulky para-aortic nodes compress the inferior vena cava and the iliac veins. A young man with bilateral leg oedema and back pain needs his testes examined. SRB's checklist of metastatic symptomsHaemoptysis, altered breath sounds and pleural effusion; bone pain and tenderness; nodular secondaries in the liver; and central nervous system involvement.SRB 26 · p.1072 SRB adds that in 10% of cases it presents asymptomatically, found incidentally.SRB 26 · p.1072
6. Any breast enlargement, or change in body hair or libido? Because a hormone-producing tumour declares itself this way. B&L: "around 5% of cases have gynaecomastia (mainly NSGCT)."B&L 86 · p.1571 SRB agrees and gives the mechanism: "gynaecomastia may be present in few teratomas, 5%. It is due to raised beta-HCG."SRB 26 · p.1072 The two sex cord-stromal tumours, and the mnemonic that works Leydig masculinises, Sertoli feminises. SRB: Leydig cell tumour is a prepubertal tumour with "excessive output of androgens causing sexual precocity, extreme muscular development often mimicking infant hercules"; Sertoli cell tumour is postpubertal and "causes feminising effect with gynaecomastia, loss of libido and aspermia".SRB 26 · p.1071 S Das puts it the same way.Das 40 · p.630 And the treatment point SRB addsThe Leydig cell tumour is "radioresistant and chemoresistant", so surgery is the only treatment.SRB 26 · p.1071 B&L agrees in principle: "most of these tumours are benign (around 80%), so conservative treatment of small lesions with organ-sparing surgery is feasible, if the diagnosis is considered."B&L 86 · p.1572

3Examination: five findings, each with its reason

1. Is the swelling purely scrotal, and can you get above it? S Das: "on examination, the swelling is purely scrotal."Das 40 · p.630 You can get above a testicular tumour, which separates it at once from an inguinoscrotal hernia, and it does not transilluminate, which separates it from a hydrocele unless there is a secondary one. S Das's warning about the torchDo it in darkness, and place the pencil torch laterally over the swollen scrotum, with the rolled paper on the other side. A red glow throughout the scrotum means clear fluid.Das 40 · p.621
The error to avoid: putting the torch on the posterior aspect with the paper in front. The testis then comes in the way of the light and the test reads false negative, so a genuine hydrocele looks solid.Das 40 · p.621
2. What does the testis itself feel like? S Das distinguishes the two tumours here, with the caution that it is not reliable: "the testis is enlarged, firm, smooth and heavy. This is more noticed in case of seminoma, but slight nodularity can be felt. In teratoma the surface is irregular or nodular. Consistency may be varying with soft bosses in between."Das 40 · p.630 And he states the limit plainly: "clinically it may not be possible to differentiate between seminoma from teratoma and final differentiation rests on histology."Das 40 · p.630 The word to useHeavy. Weight out of proportion to size is the oldest sign of a testicular tumour and the one examiners listen for. B&L's formulation is "an intratesticular solid mass", and its summary box reduces the whole case to: "a solid testicular lump that cannot be felt separately from the testis may be a malignant tumour."B&L 86 · p.1571
3. Is testicular sensation present? Gentle pressure on a normal testis produces a characteristic sickening discomfort referred to the epigastrium. S Das: "in gumma and malignant tumour of the testis, the testicular sensation quickly dwindles away (more so in case of gumma)."Das 40 · p.622 And of tumours specifically: "testicular sensation is always lost early, but one must be very gentle in finding out this sign."Das 40 · p.630 SRB lists "loss of testicular sensation (in early stage only)" among its findings.SRB 26 · p.1071 Be careful how you claim itS Das elsewhere writes that testicular sensation "is always absent in testicular tumours",Das 40 · p.626 which is the stronger claim. The sign is useful when lost; its presence does not exclude a tumour, and the whole sign is absent from Bailey & Love. Use it to support your diagnosis, never to abandon one. And elicit it gently: this is a painful test done badly.
4. Feel the cord, and feel the vas separately This is the single most useful discriminator against infection, and SRB names it: "sign of vas: to differentiate tumour from infection, in testicular tumours vas is normal, cord structures may become bulky because of cremasteric hypertrophy whereas in infection vas is thickened, beaded, tender."SRB 26 · p.1072 S Das says the same: "the spermatic cord remains normal for quite a long time. But eventually it may be thickened due to cremasteric hypertrophy and enlargement of testicular vessels, but the vas is never thickened."Das 40 · p.630 The logicA tumour is confined by the tunica albuginea and spreads along lymphatics, which do not thicken the vas. Tuberculous epididymitis spreads along the vas itself, which becomes thickened and beaded from subepithelial tubercles. One palpates a tube, the other does not. And do a rectal examinationS Das: "rectal examination will reveal no abnormality of the prostate and seminal vesicles."Das 40 · p.630 SRB: "vas, prostate and seminal vesicles are normal."SRB 26 · p.1071 A normal finding here is positive evidence against genitourinary tuberculosis, which is why you do it.
5. Then examine for secondaries, and in the right places S Das: "lymphatic metastasis will cause enlargement of the pre- and para-aortic groups of lymph nodes which are situated just above the level of the umbilicus. Liver should be palpated. Lung should be examined including chest X-ray to exclude blood-borne metastasis there."Das 40 · p.630 SRB describes exactly how the nodal mass feels: "often in epigastric region para-aortic lymph nodes may be palpable as hard, nodular, nontender, nonmobile, vertically placed, resonant mass (not moving with respiration)."SRB 26 · p.1072 Do not examine the groin and call it stagingThis is the classic error. B&L: "the lymphatic drainage of the testes is to the para-aortic lymph nodes near the origin of the gonadal vessels. The contralateral para-aortic lymph nodes are sometimes involved by tumour spread, but the inguinal lymph nodes are affected only if the scrotal skin is involved."B&L 86 · p.1569 The embryological reason is the one to give: the testis descends from the posterior abdominal wall and takes its lymphatic drainage with it, so the first-echelon nodes are para-aortic, not inguinal. SRB adds that previous scrotal or inguinal surgery can also open the inguinal route.SRB 26 · p.1072 And the supraclavicular fossaSRB: from the retroperitoneal and para-aortic nodes, spread goes on "to left supraclavicular nodes and posterior mediastinal nodes".SRB 26 · p.1071
The primary landing zone, which separates a good answer from a very good one SRB gives the side-specific first nodes, and no other book here does.SRB 26 · p.1071

Right testicular tumour: interaortocaval nodes immediately below the renal vessels (L2 level) as the primary landing zone, then para-aortic, paracaval, preaortic and common iliac.
Left testicular tumour: true para-aortic nodes just below the renal vessels, then preaortic and common iliac.

And one more route worth knowing, because it explains iliac nodes in a testis tumour: "lymphatics along the medial side of testis may run with the artery of vas draining into the common iliac nodes at the bifurcation of common iliac artery."SRB 26 · p.1071

4Differential diagnosis

ConditionWhat separates it
Testicular tumourSolid, heavy, testis not felt separately, testicular sensation lost, vas normal, no transillumination, cord may be bulky from cremasteric hypertrophy
Vaginal hydroceleFluctuant, transilluminates, testis cannot be felt separately because fluid surrounds it. Remember a tumour can have a secondary hydrocele: SRB and B&L both say it is common, so a hydrocele that will not transilluminate fully, or in a young man, must be imagedSRB 26 · p.1071B&L 86 · p.1571
Acute epididymo-orchitisPainful, tender, febrile, vas thickened and tender, and it settles on antibiotics. A tumour with intratumoural haemorrhage can mimic itB&L 86 · p.1571
Tuberculous epididymitisBegins in the epididymis, especially the globus minor; vas beaded from subepithelial tubercles; prostate and seminal vesicles may be indurated on rectal examination; a secondary hydrocele in about 30% of casesSRB 26 · p.1059
Acute or chronic haematoceleHistory of trauma or of repeated aspiration; S Das notes the absence of gradual enlargement, preserved testicular sensation and absence of metastases favour haematoceleDas 40 · p.626
Gumma of the testisPainless, hard, testicular sensation lost early and more completely than in a tumour; the testis later softens; a secondary hydrocele is almost always presentDas 40 · pp.622, 628
Torsion of the testisA surgical emergency, not a differential to work through at leisure. Sudden severe pain; the affected testis lies higher than its fellowSRB 26 · p.1071 Direction, as SRB teaches it: the right testis rotates clockwise, the left anticlockwise.SRB 26 · p.1068
Explore on clinical suspicion. B&L: Doppler "is not routinely recommended", and "if there is any doubt as to the diagnosis, then urgent scrotal exploration is indicated". Salvage is nearly 100% within 6 hours against 20% at 24 hours.B&L 86 · pp.1561, 1562 At exploration the testis is untwisted, viability checked, and SRB's rule applied: "when in doubt, always testis is left in place and observed", with orchidectomy only after consent.SRB 26 · p.1069
Epididymal cystFelt separately from the testis, behind and above it; multilocular; brilliantly transilluminant, finely tessellated like a Chinese lanternDas 40 · p.630
Which way does a torsed testis twist? An SRB page-footer line contradicts SRB's own text, and modern teaching differs again
SRB's text, which is the answer to give
The right testis rotates clockwise and the left anticlockwise. This is in the body of SRB's torsion section and is what an Indian examiner is marking against.SRB 26 · p.1068
The line at the foot of SRB p.1073
A one-line quotation sits at the bottom of a page about retroperitoneal node dissection: "In torsion testis, testis always twists away from midline", attributed to John P Sparks.SRB 26 · p.1073 SRB prints several of these epigrams as page furniture. It is not part of the torsion teaching, and it does not agree with SRB's own text above.
Bailey & Love
Gives no direction at all. It is concerned with the twist's extent and duration: 720° causes ischaemia faster than 360°, and the window is 6 hours.B&L 86 · p.1561
Outside the three books
Not from S Das, Bailey & Love or SRB, and flagged as such: standard surgical teaching elsewhere is that the testis usually rotates medially, which is why manual detorsion is described as turning it outwards, like opening a book. Neither of these books describes manual detorsion at all. Do not volunteer this in place of SRB's answer.
How to answer: give SRB's text — right clockwise, left anticlockwise. If you are pressed on manual detorsion, say that the books you are quoting do not describe it, that the definitive treatment is urgent exploration, untwisting, viability check and bilateral fixation, and that imaging must not delay it. The direction is never the point the examiner is testing; the six-hour window is.

5Investigations: the order matters as much as the list

The three prohibitions, first
SRB states them as a heading, and they are worth a mark each: "No FNAC; no scrotal approach; no incision biopsy."SRB 26 · p.1073
WhyA needle or an incision through the scrotal skin breaches the tunica and opens the inguinal and scrotal lymphatics, which are not the tumour's natural route. That converts a disease staged and treated through the para-aortic nodes into one with unpredictable inguinal spread, and it changes the field for any later radiotherapy. B&L makes the same point from the anatomy: the inguinal nodes are involved "only if the scrotal skin is involved".B&L 86 · p.1569
Ultrasound of the scrotum, and it is mandatory
B&L: "the diagnosis is confirmed by ultrasound scanning of the testis, which is also able to assess the contralateral testis. It is a mandatory test in all suspected cases of testicular tumour."B&L 86 · p.1571 Its summary box repeats it: "ultrasound is a mandatory investigation in all cases of suspected testicular tumour."B&L 86 · p.1571 Say mandatory and say both testes.
Tumour markers, taken before orchidectomy
B&L is explicit about the timing: "blood is taken prior to orchidectomy to measure the levels of tumour markers, which are raised in around 50% of cases."B&L 86 · p.1571
Why beforeBecause the post-operative fall is the measurement that tells you whether all tumour has gone, and you cannot interpret a fall without a baseline. B&L: "the mean serum half-lives of AFP and HCG are 5 to 7 days and 2 to 3 days, respectively, and reassessment of the markers following orchidectomy can indicate whether all the tumour tissue has been removed."B&L 86 · p.1571 SRB's half-life for beta-HCG is 18 to 36 hours, which is the figure Indian papers expect.SRB 26 · p.1073
The three markers, and what each means
AFP, from yolk sac elements. SRB: "raised AFP always indicates teratomatous tumour. AFP level increase is not seen in pure seminomas."SRB 26 · p.1073 That is the single most examined sentence about markers: a raised AFP means it is not a pure seminoma, whatever the histology says.
Beta-HCG, from syncytiotrophoblast. SRB: "beta-HCG is never found in normal individual. It is secreted by syncytiotrophoblasts", and it is raised in choriocarcinoma 100%, embryonal carcinoma 65%, teratoma, and in recurrent or residual disease.SRB 26 · p.1073
LDH, a burden marker rather than a tissue marker. B&L: "lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is expressed on chromosome 12p, which is often amplified in testis cancer cells. LDH is less specific for testis cancer than HCG or AFP. However, elevated LDH levels are associated with high tumour burden in seminoma and recurrence in NSGCT."B&L 86 · p.1571
PLAP, which only SRB gives: "placental alkaline phosphatase (PLAP) is increased in seminoma."SRB 26 · p.1073 It does not appear in B&L 28e's chapter, so offer it as a seminoma marker but do not rest an answer on it.
The percentages differ between booksSee the amber box on markers. Give the pattern, not a bare number.
Staging imaging
CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis. B&L: "while a chest radiograph can show the 'classical' cannonball metastases, CT scanning of the chest, abdomen and pelvis has taken over as the most useful means of detecting metastases and monitoring the response to therapy."B&L 86 · p.1571 Its summary box: "CT scanning of chest, abdomen and pelvis is central to the staging of testicular tumours."B&L 86 · p.1572 SRB agrees, calling CT better than ultrasound for the abdomen and HRCT ideal for the chest.SRB 26 · p.1073
Say "cannonball metastases"It is the classical chest film appearance and it is still in the book, even though CT has superseded the film for staging.
Semen analysis and sperm banking, which candidates forget
B&L puts it first under Treatment: "men should be offered semen analysis and sperm banking prior to interventions such as surgery and chemotherapy that may render them infertile."B&L 86 · p.1572 These are young men with a curable cancer. Offering fertility preservation before treatment is part of the correct answer, not an afterthought.
Risk-group classification, which SRB expects by name
Based on AFP, beta-HCG, LDH and the presence of non-pulmonary visceral secondaries in bone, liver or brain: good risk and intermediate risk for seminomatous germ cell tumour; good, intermediate and poor risk for non-seminomatous.SRB 26 · p.1073 There is no poor-risk category for seminoma, which is the detail worth remembering.
How much does an undescended testis raise the cancer risk: fifty times, or two to six times? A live numerical disagreement of an order of magnitude, and the books also differ on whether orchidopexy helps. S Das 40 p.630 against B&L 86 p.1559
S Das
"Undescended testis is more vulnerable (about 50 times) to malignant transformation which is not reduced by late orchidopexy."Das 40 · p.630 Fifty-fold, and no benefit from operating late.
Bailey & Love 28e
Two separate figures, both an order of magnitude lower, and the timing does matter: "overall, the risk of testicular cancer if orchidopexy is done before puberty is around two to three times that of the general population. It is five to six times higher when orchidopexy is done after puberty. The risk of cancer does not seem to be different when orchidopexy is done early in infancy compared with later in childhood."B&L 86 · p.1559 It also notes the histology shifts: seminoma is "the most common type of testicular cancer in untreated undescended testes", whereas "after orchidopexy, seminomas represent only 30% of testicular tumours in previously undescended testes".B&L 86 · p.1559
Why the figures are so far apart
They are not the same quantity. The old 35 to 50 fold figures come from series of untreated, often intra-abdominal testes, where the risk is genuinely much higher. B&L's 2 to 3 and 5 to 6 fold figures are for testes that have been brought down, which is now almost every patient, and they are quoted relative to the whole male population. So S Das is describing the natural history of a neglected testis and B&L is describing the residual risk after treatment. Note also that the two books are not quite in conflict on orchidopexy: S Das says late orchidopexy does not reduce the risk, and B&L's figures agree, since post-pubertal repair leaves a 5 to 6 fold risk against 2 to 3 fold for pre-pubertal.
How to answer: give the direction and the condition, and only then a number. "An undescended testis carries a substantially increased risk of malignancy, and the commonest tumour in an untreated undescended testis is seminoma. Older series of untreated, particularly intra-abdominal, testes quote figures as high as thirty to fifty fold. After orchidopexy the residual risk is much lower: Bailey and Love gives two to three times the general population if the operation was done before puberty and five to six times if after. Orchidopexy does not abolish the risk, which is why these boys are taught testicular self-examination." If a written paper wants one number, write S Das's fifty times and qualify it in the same sentence as applying to the untreated testis. The fuller treatment of this question is in short case 19, undescended testis.
Tumour marker percentages: the two books give different figures for the same thing A live numerical disagreement, worst for beta-HCG in seminoma. B&L 86 p.1571 says around 30%; SRB 26 p.1073 says 10%
Bailey & Love 28e
"A rise in AFP is seen in around 50 to 70% of NSGCTs and a rise in HCG is seen in 40 to 60% of NSGCTs and around 30% of seminomas." Overall, markers are "raised in around 50% of cases".B&L 86 · p.1571
SRB
"AFP and beta-HCG are elevated in nonseminomatous germ cell tumours (teratomas), 65%... beta-HCG may be elevated in advanced cases of seminomas (10%)... LDH is increased in 80% of advanced seminomas and 60% of nonseminomatous germ cell tumour."SRB 26 · p.1073
Where they really differ, and where they only seem to
The NSGCT figures are compatible: SRB's 65% for the pair together sits inside B&L's 50 to 70% for AFP and 40 to 60% for HCG. The seminoma figures do not agree: 30% against 10%, a threefold gap. Part of that is the qualifier, since SRB's 10% is for advanced seminoma specifically, where you would expect the higher rather than the lower figure. The reason may be the syncytiotrophoblastic variant, which SRB itself says occurs in 15% of classic seminomas and produces high levels of beta-HCG; depending on whether a series counts those, the proportion of HCG-positive seminomas moves substantially.SRB 26 · p.1070
How to answer: answer the pattern, which no book disputes, and quote a number only if asked. The pattern: AFP is never raised in a pure seminoma, so a raised AFP means the tumour is not a pure seminoma however it looks down the microscope. Beta-HCG can be raised in either, more often and more markedly in non-seminomatous tumours, and in a minority of seminomas because of syncytiotrophoblastic elements. LDH is not tissue-specific; it reflects tumour burden and predicts recurrence. If pressed for figures, give SRB's, since an Indian paper is marked against SRB, and flag that the proportion of HCG-positive seminomas is quoted anywhere between 10 and 30%. The clinically important consequence is in both books: a seminoma with high markers is treated as a non-seminomatous tumour.SRB 26 · p.1073
Is frozen section with the Chevassu manoeuvre still part of the operation? A live disagreement about operative sequence. SRB 26 p.1073 builds the operation around a frozen section; neither "Chevassu" nor "frozen section" appears in B&L 86
SRB
Lists the sequence under Investigations, not treatment, which tells you how it is conceived: "through inguinal approach, cord and testis are exposed. A soft clamp is applied to the cord at or above the level of the deep ring so as to prevent dissemination through blood. Frozen section biopsy is done from the suspected area. If tumour is positive, high orchidectomy is done (Chevassu manoeuvre)."SRB 26 · p.1073 The clamp goes on before the testis is delivered, and the decision to remove it is made on histology obtained in theatre.
Bailey & Love 28e
Neither the eponym nor the step appears. The diagnosis is made beforehand by ultrasound, which B&L calls mandatory, and the operation is then committed: "the orchidectomy is undertaken via an inguinal incision. The spermatic cord is displayed by dividing the external oblique aponeurosis and a soft clamp is placed across the cord to stop dissemination of malignant cells as the testis is mobilised into the wound. If there is a tumour the cord should be double transfixed and divided at the level of the internal inguinal ring and the testis removed."B&L 86 · pp.1571, 1572 The soft clamp is identical. What has gone is the intraoperative histology.
Why the step has faded
High-resolution scrotal ultrasound now makes the diagnosis of a solid intratesticular mass reliably enough that an on-table decision is rarely needed, and 99% of such masses are malignant anyway. Where frozen section survives is testis-sparing surgery for a small lesion where a benign diagnosis is genuinely possible, which B&L describes for sex cord-stromal tumours and for children with a normal AFP: "a normal AFP level in children suggests a strong likelihood of a benign tumour. For such tumours, as in cases of epidermoid cysts, testis-sparing surgery of the mass rather than radical orchidectomy can be considered."B&L 86 · p.1572
How to answer: give the three steps that both books share and mention the eponym as an option rather than a requirement. "I would do a radical orchidectomy through an inguinal incision, never a scrotal one. I would open the external oblique aponeurosis, apply a soft clamp to the cord at or above the deep ring before mobilising the testis into the wound so as to prevent dissemination, and then double transfix and divide the cord at the level of the internal ring. Where the diagnosis is in doubt, a frozen section can be taken before committing to orchidectomy, which is the Chevassu manoeuvre." Learn the eponym, because an Indian examiner will ask for it by name and SRB teaches it, but do not make it a necessary step: with a mandatory pre-operative ultrasound and raised markers, the diagnosis is usually not in doubt. The non-negotiable parts are inguinal incision, soft clamp before mobilisation, cord divided at the internal ring.

6Pathology and classification

The simplest classification that answers the question
Germ cell (90 to 95%), divided into seminomatous and non-seminomatous; and non-germ-cell (5 to 10%): sex cord-stromal tumours, lymphoma, and the rest. B&L's version gives the proportions: GCTs 90 to 95%; sex cord-stromal tumours 1 to 2%; lymphoma 3 to 7%; other tumours 1 to 2%.B&L 86 · p.1569 SRB's incidence list is the one Indian papers quote: seminoma 40%, teratoma 32%, seminoma plus teratoma 14%, interstitial tumours 1.5%, lymphoma 7%.SRB 26 · p.1070 S Das gives seminoma 40%, teratoma 35%, mixed 15%, lymphoma 6%, interstitial 2%, other 2%.Das 40 · p.630
Seminoma: what it looks like and what it means
Gross. "A seminoma typically has a cut surface that is homogeneous and pinkish cream in colour. It appears to compress neighbouring testicular tissue."B&L 86 · p.1569 SRB: "lobulated, fleshy, homogeneous, creamy or pinkish" and starting "in the mediastinum of testis and lower pole".SRB 26 · p.1070
Microscopy. "It consists of oval cells with clear cytoplasm and large, rounded nuclei with prominent acidophilic nucleoli. Sheets of cells resembling spermatocytes are separated by a fine fibrous stroma."B&L 86 · p.1569
The one prognostic detail to add"Active lymphocytic infiltration of the tumour suggests a good host response and a better prognosis."B&L 86 · p.1569 SRB mentions the same lymphocytic infiltrate.SRB 26 · p.1070 It is the kind of detail that distinguishes an answer.
Spread. "Seminomas metastasise mainly via the lymphatics and haematogenous spread is uncommon."B&L 86 · p.1569 S Das: "seminomas first metastasise by lymphatic spread and bloodborne metastasis is late; whereas in teratomas blood-borne metastasis is early."Das 40 · p.630 That single contrast explains why the two are staged and treated differently.
Proportion and age. "Seminoma accounts for 50% of all testicular germinal cell tumours. They seldom occur in childhood, in young adults or in patients over 70 years of age."B&L 86 · p.1570
SRB's four types, which an Indian paper may ask for: typical or classic (with a syncytiotrophoblastic form in 15% producing high beta-HCG); spermatocytic, in older men, in which "spread is very rare"; anaplastic, with "high mitotic index, nuclear pleomorphism, anaplasia with high potentiality to spread"; and atypical.SRB 26 · p.1070 On spermatocytic seminoma the two books now part company, which the amber box below sets out.
The non-seminomatous tumours, and the marker each produces
B&L's four, "which may coexist within a single tumour":B&L 86 · p.1569
Embryonal carcinoma. "Highly malignant tumours that occasionally invade cord structures."B&L 86 · p.1569
Yolk sac tumour. Produces AFP. "It appears as a single tumour type in children and part of a mixed tumour in adults."B&L 86 · pp.1569, 1570 SRB adds the histology detail: the endodermal sinus tumour "contains Schiller-Duval bodies".SRB 26 · p.1070
Teratoma. "Teratomas consist of different tissues derived from ectoderm, endoderm and mesoderm."B&L 86 · p.1570 SRB: "it arises from totipotent cells", the cut surface shows "solid and cystic spaces with areas of haemorrhage... gelatinous fluid and cartilaginous nodules", and "teratoma spreads mainly through blood, less commonly through lymphatics".SRB 26 · p.1070
Choriocarcinoma. Produces beta-HCG. "This is part of a testicular GCT in 25% of tumours in adults. It very seldom appears as the single tumour component... this is a highly malignant tumour that metastasises early via both the lymphatics and the bloodstream."B&L 86 · p.1570
And how teratoma is subclassified, which has changedSee the amber box: B&L has abandoned the mature and immature split that SRB still teaches, and SRB additionally gives the four British Testicular Tumour Panel types.
The sex cord-stromal tumours, with the figures
Leydig cell tumour, the commonest of them: "1 to 3% of adult testicular tumours and 3% of testicular tumours in infants and children. These tumours occur in about 8% of patients with Klinefelter's syndrome... most of these tumours are benign. Malignant transformation occurs in 10% and is related to increased size (over 5 cm), increased cellular atypia, increased cell proliferation, necrosis, vessel invasion and DNA aneuploidy."B&L 86 · p.1570
Sertoli cell tumour: "less than 1% of testicular tumours, and the mean age at diagnosis is around 45 years... rarely, these occur in patients with androgen insensitivity syndrome and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. The rate of malignancy ranges between 10% and 22%."B&L 86 · p.1570
Granulosa cell tumour: "extremely rare in adult men, but a juvenile type accounts for 6% of testis tumours in childhood."B&L 86 · p.1571
Gonadoblastoma, the mixed germ cell and sex cord tumour: "seen in individuals with mixed gonadal dysgenesis (risk 15 to 25%), which is associated with cryptorchidism, hypospadias, gynaecomastia or female internal genitalia. It seldom occurs in phenotypical and genotypical males."B&L 86 · p.1571
Tumours in children are a different disease
"Paediatric testicular tumours are distinct from adult testicular tumours. GCTs in adults represent about 95% of all testicular tumours but only 60 to 75% in children. The most common malignant tumour in children is the yolk sac tumour, which is very rare in its pure form in adults." And the marker drives the decision: "surgical treatment usually begins with radical orchidectomy, which is often recommended whenever the AFP level is elevated (suggesting the presence of a yolk sac tumour at age over 1 year). A normal AFP level in children suggests a strong likelihood of a benign tumour."B&L 86 · p.1572
SRB's two terms that B&L does not use
Hurricane type: "a very aggressive, highly malignant testicular tumour which is more often fatal in few weeks."SRB 26 · p.1072 And SRB names the other classifications an examiner may mention: Dixon and Moore, WHO, and the British tumour panel.SRB 26 · p.1070 Neither "hurricane" nor "Dixon" appears in B&L 28e's chapter, so recognise them without relying on them.
How is a teratoma classified? The British panel's four types, or no subclassification at all? Part live disagreement, part a change B&L states outright. SRB 26 p.1070 gives four types and the mature/immature split; B&L 86 p.1570 says that split "has been abandoned"
SRB
Gives both systems on the same page. First the broad one: "teratoma can be mature; immature; choriocarcinoma or mixed germ cell tumour." Then the British Testicular Tumour Panel's four histological types with their frequencies: "1. Teratoma differentiated (1%). 2. Teratoma intermediate (30%) common, two subtypes are A and B. Type A contains matured cells but type B is more malignant consisting of less proper differentiated tissues. 3. Teratoma anaplastic (15%), secretes alpha-fetoprotein. 4. Teratoma trophoblastic (1%), it shows high levels of beta-HCG."SRB 26 · p.1070
Bailey & Love 28e
Describes the tissues and then deletes the classification: "immature components are often neuroectodermal or mesenchymal tissue, while more mature tissue is often cystic with epithelial differentiation or consists of smooth muscle, connective tissue or cartilage. Since most teratomas consist of a mixture of tissues, the old separation into mature and immature types has been abandoned. All can metastasise."B&L 86 · p.1570 The British Testicular Tumour Panel is not named, and none of the subtype phrases appears: not teratoma differentiated, teratoma intermediate, teratoma anaplastic, teratoma trophoblastic, nor the abbreviations MTU and MTI. The word "differentiated" does occur twice in the chapter, but both times as an ordinary verb, of distinguishing a retractile testis from a true undescended one and of distinguishing idiopathic scrotal oedema from torsion, never as the name of a grade.
What changed, and why it matters clinically
The panel's system was built to predict behaviour from histology, so that a well-differentiated teratoma could be treated less aggressively. B&L's last four words destroy that premise: all can metastasise. Since most teratomas are mixtures, a specimen labelled by its predominant tissue tells you little, and modern management is driven instead by stage, markers and lymphovascular invasion, not by the teratoma subtype. That is why B&L's management section stratifies NSGCT by lymphovascular invasion rather than by histological grade.B&L 86 · p.1572
How to answer: this one depends on who is asking, so prepare both and lead with the reasoning. For an Indian written paper or a viva from an Indian textbook, give SRB's four British panel types with their percentages, because that is what the question expects and what the marking scheme contains. Then add the sentence that shows you know the current position: "The British Testicular Tumour Panel classification is the one classically taught. Current practice has moved away from subclassifying teratomas, because most are mixtures of tissues and all of them can metastasise, so management is decided by stage, by tumour markers and by the presence of lymphovascular invasion rather than by histological subtype." Do not volunteer that the classification has been abandoned without first giving it; and do not call a teratoma benign because it is well differentiated.
Spermatocytic seminoma: a variant of seminoma, or a separate tumour? Mostly an edition note. SRB 26 p.1070 lists it as a type of seminoma; B&L 86 p.1570 says it is "now considered to be a separate tumour type"
SRB
Lists it among the types of seminoma, under the seminomatous germ cell tumours: "spermatocytic seminoma occurs in older people with different phases of spermatogonia. Spread in this type is very rare."SRB 26 · p.1070
Bailey & Love 28e
Gives it its own heading and reclassifies it: "this tumour was earlier believed to be a variant of seminoma, but is now considered to be a separate tumour type, accounting for 1 to 2% of all GCTs of the testis. Only seen in adult men usually over 50 years old, they rarely metastasise; therefore, an orchidectomy is the only necessary treatment, even in large tumours. Development of sarcomas has been reported when left untreated for long time."B&L 86 · p.1570
What follows from it
The clinical teaching is the same in both books, that it barely metastasises. B&L just draws the explicit management conclusion that SRB leaves implicit: because it so rarely spreads, orchidectomy alone is enough even for a large one, with no adjuvant radiotherapy and no chemotherapy. That is the only seminomatous tumour of which that is true.
How to answer: describe it and give the management, and note the reclassification in a clause. "Spermatocytic seminoma is a tumour of men over fifty which rarely metastasises. It was classically regarded as a variant of seminoma and is now considered a separate tumour type. Orchidectomy alone is sufficient treatment, even for a large tumour, with no adjuvant therapy, which distinguishes it from classical seminoma." If asked to list the types of seminoma in a written paper, include it as SRB does, since that is the expected answer, and add the reclassification as a note.

7Staging

The clinical four-stage system SRB expects
I. Lesion confined to the testis. II. Nodes involved below the diaphragm. III. Nodes involved above the diaphragm. IV. Distant, blood-borne spread.SRB 26 · p.1072 Easy to recite, easy to draw, and the one to write if the question says "stage a testicular tumour".
The TNM elements worth knowing
T1 limited to testis and epididymis, no vascular or lymphatic invasion, may invade tunica albuginea but not tunica vaginalis. T2 the same but with vascular or lymphatic invasion, or extending through tunica albuginea into tunica vaginalis. T3 invades spermatic cord. T4 invades scrotum.SRB 26 · p.1072
N by node size: N1 not more than 2 cm; N2 2 to 5 cm; N3 over 5 cm.SRB 26 · p.1072
M1a non-regional nodes or lung; M1b elsewhere.SRB 26 · p.1072
The S category, which is unique to this cancerTestis is one of the few sites where serum markers are part of the stage. S0 normal; S1 LDH under 1.5 times normal and HCG under 5000 mIU/mL and AFP under 1000 ng/mL; S2 LDH 1.5 to 10 times normal, or HCG 5000 to 50 000, or AFP 1000 to 10 000.SRB 26 · p.1072 Saying that markers are built into the staging system, and that this is unusual, is worth a mark on its own.
How many patients present early
B&L: "between 75% and 80% of patients with seminoma and about 55 to 64% of patients with NSGCT have stage I disease at diagnosis."B&L 86 · p.1572 So most present with disease confined to the testis, which is why the cure rates are what they are.
Are there four stages or three? A live disagreement with a real trap: "stage III" means different things. SRB 26 p.1072 gives four stages; B&L 86 p.1572 gives three
SRB
Four, split at the diaphragm, with blood-borne spread as a separate stage: "I. Lesion confined to testis. II. Nodes involved below the diaphragm. III. Nodes involved above the diaphragm. IV. Distant (blood) spread."SRB 26 · p.1072 SRB then also gives the full TNM with stage groupings to IIIC, where distant metastasis sits in stage III, so SRB's own two systems do not quite agree with each other.SRB 26 · p.1073
Bailey & Love 28e
Three prognostic groups, and no stage IV: "prognostic groups can be defined according to non-metastatic (stage I) and metastatic disease (lymph node metastasis, stage II; distant metastasis or nodal metastasis with elevated tumour markers, stage III)." It then refers the detail out: "the exact classification details can be found in the TNM Classification of Malignant Tumours, 8th edn."B&L 86 · p.1572 Note what B&L puts in stage III: not only distant metastasis but also nodal disease with elevated markers. And its management strategies are "adapted from the European Association of Urology's current guidelines".B&L 86 · p.1572
Where the trap is
In SRB's clinical system, stage III means supradiaphragmatic nodes and stage IV means blood-borne spread. In B&L and in TNM 8, stage III means distant metastasis, with no stage IV at all. So a bare "stage III" describes a different patient in each book, and a candidate who says "stage IV" to an examiner working from TNM has used a category that no longer exists.
How to answer: name the system, then stage the patient. For an Indian examination, write SRB's four clinical stages, because that is the expected answer, and label it: "On the clinical staging system: stage I confined to the testis, II nodes below the diaphragm, III nodes above the diaphragm, IV blood-borne metastasis." Then add one sentence to show you know the current one: "The TNM eighth edition classification used in current practice has three stages, with distant metastasis as stage III, and it uniquely incorporates serum tumour markers as an S category." That last point about markers in the staging system is the strongest thing you can say here, because it is true in both systems and most candidates do not know it.

8Treatment

Step one for everybody: radical inguinal orchidectomy
Both books describe the same operation. B&L: "the orchidectomy is undertaken via an inguinal incision. The spermatic cord is displayed by dividing the external oblique aponeurosis and a soft clamp is placed across the cord to stop dissemination of malignant cells as the testis is mobilised into the wound. If there is a tumour the cord should be double transfixed and divided at the level of the internal inguinal ring and the testis removed."B&L 86 · p.1572 SRB: high orchidectomy through the inguinal approach, with the cord ligated at or above the internal ring, not through a scrotal incision.SRB 26 · p.1074
The three things to say, in orderInguinal, not scrotal. Clamp the cord before you mobilise the testis. Divide the cord at the internal ring. Each has a reason: the incision avoids opening the scrotal lymphatics; the clamp prevents venous dissemination while the tumour is handled; and dividing high removes the full length of cord that could carry tumour, and leaves a stump that can be found again at a later retroperitoneal dissection.
Then treatment by histology and stage
B&L states why the outlook is good: "the treatment of patients with GCTs of the testis is usually successful, even in advanced cases. This largely reflects the excellent response of these tumours to chemotherapy and (for seminomatous tumours) to radiotherapy."B&L 86 · p.1572 Its summary box: "testicular tumours are extremely sensitive to platinum-based chemotherapy" and "prognosis is excellent when the patient is treated with combination chemotherapy in a cancer centre."B&L 86 · p.1572
Stage I seminoma: three options, and the choice has changed
The risk you are treating: "about 15% of patients with clinical stage I seminoma have subclinical metastatic disease, usually in the retroperitoneum, and will relapse after orchidectomy alone."B&L 86 · p.1572
Surveillance. "Recurrence rates of 6% have been described in patients with low-risk features, including tumour size under 4 cm and no stromal rete testis invasion, with cancer-specific survival rate reported with surveillance at over 95%. The main limitation of surveillance is the need for intensive follow-up."B&L 86 · p.1572
Adjuvant carboplatin. "One course of adjuvant carboplatin therapy compared with radiotherapy shows no significant difference in recurrence rate, time to recurrence and survival after a median follow-up of 4 years."B&L 86 · p.1572
Adjuvant radiotherapy. "Seminomas are radiosensitive. Radiotherapy to a para-aortic field or to para-aortic and ipsilateral iliac nodes reduces the relapse rate to 1 to 3%. The rate of severe radiation toxicity is under 2%. The main concern is the long-term risk of secondary malignancies."B&L 86 · p.1572
And this is where the books divergeSee the amber box. SRB calls radiotherapy the treatment of choice; B&L no longer does.
Stage I NSGCT: three options, and here the balance has also shifted
The risk: "up to 50% of patients with NSGCT with clinical stage I disease have subclinical metastases and will relapse during surveillance."B&L 86 · p.1572
Surveillance, for selected patients: "14 to 48% of CSI-NSGCT patients undergoing surveillance have recurrence within 2 years of orchidectomy. Careful surveillance can be an option for compliant, risk-stratified (based on the presence of lymphovascular invasion) patients who are well informed about the expected recurrence rate as well as the salvage treatment."B&L 86 · p.1572 Note the stratifier: lymphovascular invasion.
Adjuvant chemotherapy: "one cycle of bleomycin-etoposide-cisplatin (BEP) is now the recommended strategy with recurrence rates of around 3%. The very long-term side effects, particularly cardiovascular, remain to be ascertained."B&L 86 · p.1572
RPLND: its role "has now decreased". See the amber box.
Metastatic disease, stages II and III
"Treatment for metastatic testicular cancer is chemotherapy. Previously, radiotherapy was often used for early stage II seminoma but the cardiovascular and second malignancy risks have led to chemotherapy (three cycles of BEP or four cycles of etoposide and cisplatin) being the preferred alternative... the initial treatment is chemotherapy (BEP) in all advanced cases of NSGCT except postpubertal teratoma without elevated tumour markers, which can be managed by RPLND surgery."B&L 86 · p.1572 SRB's regimen is the same: "BEP regimen is commonly used", with cisplatin, bleomycin, vinblastine, etoposide, ifosfamide, mesna and paclitaxel among the available drugs.SRB 26 · p.1074
RPLND: what it removes and what it costs
SRB describes the field in detail, which is what an Indian examiner will ask for: "removal of precaval, retrocaval, paracaval, interaortocaval, retroaortic, para-aortic, common iliac nodes along with removal of gonadal vein and adjacent fibrofatty tissues from internal ring level to its insertion into renal vein on left side and inferior vena cava on right side."SRB 26 · p.1073
Mortality 1%. Complications: haemorrhage; injury to major vessels, ureter or bowel; chylous ascites; lymphocele; and retrograde ejaculation.SRB 26 · p.1074
The modification that exists only to save ejaculation"Modified RPLND is same side lymph node dissection both above and below the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA); opposite side dissection is limited to above the level of IMA so that sympathetic chain on opposite side is preserved to retain ejaculation."SRB 26 · p.1074 SRB adds that nerve sparing RPLND is ideal if technically possible, done on the side opposite the tumour, and that laparoscopic RPLND is also advocated safely.SRB 26 · p.1074 The anatomical point to say is that ejaculation depends on the sympathetic chain and the hypogastric plexus, which lie in the field of dissection.
Follow-up and prognosis
SRB: "measurement of tumour markers at regular intervals for 5 years and yearly after 5 years. CT abdomen and chest once a year."SRB 26 · p.1074 Prognosis depends on histology and stage: SRB gives stage II 90% and stage III 70% five-year survival.SRB 26 · p.1074 B&L's framing is that prognosis is excellent with combination chemotherapy in a cancer centre.B&L 86 · p.1572
Stage I seminoma: is radiotherapy the treatment of choice? A live disagreement, and the one that has moved most. SRB 26 p.1073 says radiotherapy is the treatment of choice; B&L 86 p.1572 offers three equivalent options and flags radiotherapy's long-term risk
SRB
Unqualified: "seminomas are radiosensitive. So after high orchidectomy, radiotherapy is given to increase the cure rate and also to reduce relapse. It is the treatment of choice in stage I seminomas. Opposite testis should be shielded during radiotherapy."SRB 26 · p.1073 Chemotherapy is mentioned as "also effective", with cisplatin named, and surveillance is not offered as an option at all.
Bailey & Love 28e
Puts three options side by side and ranks none as the choice. It confirms that seminomas are radiosensitive and that radiotherapy "reduces the relapse rate to 1 to 3%" with "the rate of severe radiation toxicity under 2%", and then adds the sentence that has changed practice: "the main concern is the long-term risk of secondary malignancies."B&L 86 · p.1572 It notes that one course of carboplatin is equivalent to radiotherapy on recurrence, time to recurrence and survival, and that surveillance in low-risk disease (under 4 cm, no stromal rete testis invasion) gives 6% recurrence with over 95% cancer-specific survival.B&L 86 · p.1572 For stage II seminoma it goes further and states the reversal explicitly: "previously, radiotherapy was often used for early stage II seminoma but the cardiovascular and second malignancy risks have led to chemotherapy... being the preferred alternative."B&L 86 · p.1572
Why it changed
Not because radiotherapy stopped working. It works extremely well: 1 to 3% relapse. The problem is that these are men in their thirties who will be cured and then live for fifty years, long enough for a radiation-induced second cancer and for cardiovascular damage to appear. When an alternative with the same cancer outcome exists, the late toxicity decides. That logic, equal cure, less late harm, is the whole answer.
How to answer: give the three options and the reason the ranking changed, which is a better answer than either book alone. "Stage I seminoma is highly curable whichever option is chosen, because about 85% are already cured by orchidectomy alone. There are three strategies: surveillance, which in low-risk disease, under 4 cm with no stromal rete testis invasion, carries about 6% recurrence and over 95% cancer-specific survival but demands intensive follow-up; a single course of adjuvant carboplatin; and adjuvant para-aortic radiotherapy, which reduces relapse to 1 to 3%. Seminoma is radiosensitive and radiotherapy was the classical treatment of choice, which is what SRB teaches. Current guidelines no longer rank it first, because the long-term risk of a second malignancy and of cardiovascular disease matters in a young man who will be cured, and carboplatin gives equivalent cancer outcomes." If asked for one answer in an Indian written paper, write radiotherapy, with the opposite testis shielded, as SRB does, and add surveillance and carboplatin as current alternatives. Never omit the shielding: it is a free mark.
Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection in stage I NSGCT: a major role, or a diminished one? A live disagreement with trial numbers behind it. SRB 26 p.1073 says RPLND has a major role in teratoma; B&L 86 p.1572 says its role "has now decreased"
SRB
Builds the management of teratoma around the operation, and gives a good reason: "in teratoma, retroperitoneal radical lymph node dissection (RPLND) is beneficial after high orchidectomy. Even in stage I disease, chances of existing retroperitoneal spread is 30%. So RPLND (infrahilar) has a major role especially in teratomas which are relatively radioresistant."SRB 26 · p.1073 It adds "radiotherapy is not beneficial in teratoma",SRB 26 · p.1074 which is the reason surgery carried the burden: if the tumour will not respond to radiation, the alternatives were surgery or chemotherapy.
Bailey & Love 28e
Agrees about the occult disease rate, putting it even higher at up to 50%, and then compares the two strategies head to head: "the role of this surgery has now decreased with 2-year recurrence-free survival with adjuvant BEP times 1 versus RPLND favouring chemotherapy with recurrence-free survival of 99.5% versus 91%."B&L 86 · p.1572 One cycle of BEP is "now the recommended strategy", with recurrence around 3%.B&L 86 · p.1572 RPLND survives for one specific indication: "postpubertal teratoma without elevated tumour markers, which can be managed by RPLND surgery".B&L 86 · p.1572
What actually settles it
A direct comparison: 99.5% against 91% recurrence-free survival at two years. Both books are reasoning from the same premise, that a third to a half of clinical stage I NSGCTs harbour occult retroperitoneal disease. SRB's answer was to remove the retroperitoneum; B&L's is to treat it with one cycle of chemotherapy, which also treats disease outside the dissection field and avoids retrograde ejaculation. SRB itself concedes the price, listing retrograde ejaculation among the complications and describing modified and nerve-sparing dissections designed to avoid it.SRB 26 · p.1074
How to answer: state the problem, then both solutions with the numbers. "Up to a third to a half of clinical stage I non-seminomatous tumours have occult retroperitoneal disease, so orchidectomy alone leaves a substantial relapse rate. The classical answer was retroperitoneal lymph node dissection, particularly for teratomas, which are relatively radioresistant. Current practice favours one cycle of BEP chemotherapy, which gave 99.5% against 91% two-year recurrence-free survival compared with RPLND, and avoids retrograde ejaculation. Surveillance is an option for a compliant patient stratified on lymphovascular invasion. RPLND remains indicated for a postpubertal teratoma with normal tumour markers, and for residual masses after chemotherapy." If asked to describe the operation, give SRB's field and complications, and name the modified and nerve-sparing dissections with the reason for them: preserving the sympathetic chain to retain antegrade ejaculation.

9Rapid-fire viva

What proportion of testicular swellings that are tumours are malignant?

99%. Testicular tumours are about 1% of all male malignancies but one of the commonest cancers in young men, which is why a solid intratesticular mass is treated as malignant from the outset.Das 40 · p.630B&L 86 · p.1569

Classify testicular tumours.

Germ cell tumours, 90 to 95%, divided into seminomatous and non-seminomatous. The non-seminomatous group contains embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumour, teratoma and choriocarcinoma. Non-germ-cell tumours, 5 to 10%, are the sex cord-stromal tumours (Leydig, Sertoli, granulosa), gonadoblastoma, lymphoma and secondaries.B&L 86 · p.1569SRB 26 · p.1070 By frequency, SRB: seminoma 40%, teratoma 32%, mixed 14%, lymphoma 7%, interstitial 1.5%.

Seminoma or teratoma, from the age?

Teratoma in the twenties, seminoma in the thirties and forties, with the crossover around 30.Das 40 · p.630B&L 86 · p.1569 But S Das is explicit that clinical differentiation is unreliable and the final answer rests on histology.Das 40 · p.630

Which spreads by blood and which by lymph?

Seminoma spreads mainly by lymphatics, to the para-aortic nodes, and blood-borne spread is late and uncommon. In teratoma, blood-borne spread is early.Das 40 · p.630B&L 86 · p.1569 That is why a chest CT matters particularly in a teratoma.

Where does a testicular tumour spread to first, and why not the groin?

The para-aortic nodes near the origin of the gonadal vessels, because the testis descends from the posterior abdominal wall and takes its lymphatic drainage with it. The inguinal nodes are involved only if the scrotal skin is involved, or after previous scrotal or inguinal surgery.B&L 86 · p.1569SRB 26 · p.1072

What is the primary landing zone for a right-sided tumour?

The interaortocaval nodes immediately below the renal vessels, at about L2, then the para-aortic, paracaval, preaortic and common iliac nodes. For a left-sided tumour it is the true para-aortic nodes just below the renal vessels, then preaortic and common iliac.SRB 26 · p.1071

How do you distinguish a testicular tumour from tuberculous epididymitis on examination?

The sign of the vas. In a tumour the vas is normal, though the cord may be bulky from cremasteric hypertrophy; in tuberculous infection the vas is thickened, beaded and tender, and the prostate and seminal vesicles may be indurated on rectal examination.SRB 26 · p.1072Das 40 · p.630 A tumour also begins in the body of the testis and tuberculosis in the epididymis.

A man has an epididymo-orchitis that has not settled after two weeks of antibiotics. What do you do?

Scrotal ultrasound and tumour markers. A tumour can mimic epididymo-orchitis, and acute painful enlargement from haemorrhage into a tumour can even mimic torsion.B&L 86 · p.1571Das 40 · p.630 Re-treating with antibiotics without imaging is how the diagnosis is missed.

A young man with a hydrocele. Anything you would add?

Ultrasound, to exclude an underlying tumour. A secondary hydrocele is common in testicular tumours and may prevent you palpating the testis.SRB 26 · p.1071B&L 86 · p.1571 And never aspirate or operate through the scrotum before the testis has been assessed.

What investigations, and in what order?

Scrotal ultrasound of both testes, which is mandatory. Serum tumour markers, AFP, beta-HCG and LDH, taken before orchidectomy so there is a baseline. Then CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging. Offer semen analysis and sperm banking before any treatment.B&L 86 · pp.1571, 1572 No FNAC, no scrotal approach, no incision biopsy.SRB 26 · p.1073

Why must you not do a needle biopsy or a scrotal incision?

Because breaching the scrotum opens the inguinal and scrotal lymphatics, which are not the tumour's natural route of spread. That gives the tumour access to nodes outside the para-aortic field, alters staging and alters any later radiotherapy field.SRB 26 · p.1073B&L 86 · p.1569

Which marker tells you it is not a pure seminoma?

AFP. A raised AFP always indicates a teratomatous or non-seminomatous element, and AFP is not raised in a pure seminoma.SRB 26 · p.1073 Beta-HCG can be raised in either, and a seminoma with high markers is treated as a non-seminomatous tumour.

What is LDH for?

Tumour burden, not tissue type. It is less specific than AFP or HCG, and is expressed on chromosome 12p, which is often amplified in testicular cancer cells. A raised LDH indicates high tumour burden in seminoma and predicts recurrence in NSGCT.B&L 86 · p.1571

Why are markers measured before orchidectomy?

To establish a baseline, so that the post-operative fall can be interpreted. AFP has a mean serum half-life of 5 to 7 days and HCG of 2 to 3 days, so failure of the markers to fall as predicted after orchidectomy indicates residual tumour tissue.B&L 86 · p.1571

Describe the operation.

Radical orchidectomy through an inguinal incision, never a scrotal one. The external oblique aponeurosis is divided to display the cord; a soft clamp is applied to the cord at or above the deep ring before the testis is mobilised into the wound, to prevent dissemination; the cord is then double transfixed and divided at the level of the internal ring and the testis removed.B&L 86 · p.1572SRB 26 · p.1074 Where the diagnosis is in doubt a frozen section may be taken first, the Chevassu manoeuvre.SRB 26 · p.1073

What is the Chevassu manoeuvre?

Exposing the cord and testis through an inguinal incision, applying a soft clamp to the cord at or above the deep ring, taking a frozen section from the suspicious area, and proceeding to high orchidectomy only if the frozen section confirms tumour.SRB 26 · p.1073 With a mandatory pre-operative ultrasound the step is now rarely needed, and it does not appear in Bailey and Love 28e.

Treatment of stage I seminoma.

After orchidectomy, three options. Surveillance, for low-risk disease under 4 cm with no stromal rete testis invasion, around 6% recurrence with over 95% cancer-specific survival. One course of adjuvant carboplatin. Or adjuvant radiotherapy to a para-aortic field, which cuts relapse to 1 to 3% but carries a long-term risk of second malignancy.B&L 86 · p.1572 SRB teaches radiotherapy as the treatment of choice, with the opposite testis shielded.SRB 26 · p.1073

Treatment of stage I non-seminomatous germ cell tumour.

Up to half have occult retroperitoneal disease. One cycle of BEP is the recommended adjuvant strategy, with recurrence around 3%. Surveillance is an option for a compliant patient risk-stratified on lymphovascular invasion, with 14 to 48% recurrence within two years. RPLND has a decreased role: adjuvant BEP gave 99.5% against 91% two-year recurrence-free survival.B&L 86 · p.1572

What is the BEP regimen?

Bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin. One cycle as adjuvant treatment in stage I NSGCT; three cycles, or four of etoposide and cisplatin, for metastatic disease.B&L 86 · p.1572SRB 26 · p.1074

What does an RPLND remove, and what is its characteristic complication?

The precaval, retrocaval, paracaval, interaortocaval, retroaortic, para-aortic and common iliac nodes, with the gonadal vein and adjacent fibrofatty tissue from the internal ring to the renal vein on the left or the vena cava on the right. The characteristic complication is retrograde ejaculation, from damage to the sympathetic chain and hypogastric plexus; hence modified and nerve-sparing dissections. Others are haemorrhage, injury to major vessels, ureter or bowel, chylous ascites and lymphocele. Mortality about 1%.SRB 26 · pp.1073, 1074

Which testicular tumour needs orchidectomy alone, whatever its size?

Spermatocytic seminoma. It occurs in men over fifty and very rarely metastasises, so orchidectomy is the only necessary treatment even for a large tumour. Bailey and Love now regards it as a separate tumour type rather than a variant of seminoma.B&L 86 · p.1570

Which tumour masculinises and which feminises?

The Leydig cell tumour masculinises: a prepubertal boy gets sexual precocity and marked muscular development. The Sertoli cell tumour feminises: a postpubertal man gets gynaecomastia, loss of libido and aspermia. Both are treated by surgery; the Leydig cell tumour is radioresistant and chemoresistant.SRB 26 · p.1071Das 40 · p.630

Commonest testicular tumour in a child?

The yolk sac tumour, which is very rare in pure form in adults. Germ cell tumours are only 60 to 75% of childhood testicular tumours against 95% in adults. A raised AFP suggests a yolk sac tumour and prompts radical orchidectomy; a normal AFP in a child suggests a benign tumour, where testis-sparing surgery can be considered.B&L 86 · p.1572

What would you tell a young man before you start treatment?

That the cancer is highly curable, and that treatment may affect his fertility, so he should be offered semen analysis and sperm banking before surgery or chemotherapy.B&L 86 · p.1572 That is in the book as the first line of the treatment section, and candidates routinely omit it.

How is a testicular tumour staged?

Clinically, in four stages: I confined to the testis, II nodes below the diaphragm, III nodes above the diaphragm, IV blood-borne metastasis.SRB 26 · p.1072 TNM 8, used in current practice, has three stages, with distant metastasis as stage III, and uniquely incorporates serum tumour markers as an S category.B&L 86 · p.1572SRB 26 · p.1072

What proportion present with stage I disease?

75 to 80% of seminomas and about 55 to 64% of non-seminomatous germ cell tumours.B&L 86 · p.1572 That early presentation, with the platinum sensitivity of these tumours, is why the prognosis is so much better than for most solid cancers.

Sources. S Das. A Manual on Clinical Surgery 13e (2018); Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28e; SRB's Manual of Surgery 6e. Citations give chapter and printed page. In the 28th edition of Bailey & Love the testis and scrotum are chapter 86, and the undescended testis material is at pp.1558 to 1559 in the same chapter. The clinical signs are S Das ch.40, including testicular sensation, which Bailey & Love does not describe. SRB ch.26 supplies the framework an Indian paper is marked against: the primary landing zones, the British panel teratoma types, the four clinical stages, the RPLND field and the Chevassu manoeuvre. Bailey & Love supplies current management, and it has moved a long way from the other two: it has abandoned the mature and immature teratoma classification, reclassified spermatocytic seminoma as a separate entity, replaced radiotherapy with surveillance or carboplatin in stage I seminoma, and demoted retroperitoneal lymph node dissection in favour of a single cycle of BEP. Eight amber boxes set these out. The malignancy risk of an undescended testis is covered more fully in short case 19.
